summary: I tore down 14 Japanese-learning apps and found that the ones that actually work all run the same loop — **due reviews first → a hard-capped batch of new items → immediately apply them in one sentence/story/clip → mine 1-3 words back into the deck** — and they all decompose items (radical→kanji→word→sentence) and gate new material behind prerequisites rather than dumping a level's wordlist on you. The single biggest thing a naive flashcard app misses is that "one card per word" is wrong: WaniKani asks meaning and reading as separate answers, jpdb locks a vocab card until its kanji are known, Bunpro drills grammar as typed cloze (not multiple choice), and Satori/Core2k always carry the sentence + native audio with the word. I also found a much better data foundation than the one in the shared context: **jkindrix/japanese-language-data** (CC-BY-SA 4.0) unifies KANJIDIC2, KanjiVG stroke order, JmdictFurigana (28,920 ready-to-render ruby segmentations), Kanjium pitch accent, Waller JLPT classifications (11,099 items), 14,647-word frequency ranks, a Tatoeba sentence corpus **and a `sentence-to-words` cross-reference that lets you compute true i+1 sentences offline at build time** — plus 595 hand-curated grammar points vs. OpenJLPT's ~100, which fixes the grammar-thinness problem outright. I verified every one of those files fetches and checked their shapes. I also verified ts-fsrs (23KB ESM on jsDelivr) for scheduling, and found JapanesePod101 word audio is fetchable at build time but has only ~40% coverage on N5 and no CORS header, so it must be baked plus backed by on-device `speechSynthesis`. For the business-Japanese arc, the key design insight is that keigo is a *transformation drill* and business email is *template assembly* — neither is a vocabulary list, and building them as flashcard decks is the standard failure mode.

recommendations.title: Switch the primary dataset to jkindrix/japanese-language-data and demote OpenJLPT to a cross-check
recommendations.decision: Build the content pipeline on https://github.com/jkindrix/japanese-language-data (CC-BY-SA 4.0, same license as OpenJLPT). Pull: data/enrichment/jlpt-classifications.json (11,099 Waller-sourced vocab/kanji/grammar items with level), grammar-curated/n{5..1}.json (595 grammar points with meaning_detailed, formation, formation_notes, formality, related[], examples[]), data/enrichment/furigana.json (28,920 pre-segmented ruby), data/enrichment/frequency-{corpus,subtitles,newspaper}.json (14,647 ranked), data/enrichment/pitch-accent.json, data/core/radicals.json + data/cross-refs/radical-to-kanji.json + kanji-to-radicals.json, data/enrichment/stroke-order-index.json (KanjiVG), data/corpus/sentences.json + data/cross-refs/sentence-to-words.json + word-to-sentences.json, data/grammar/conjugations.json. Keep OpenJLPT only where it has better curated example pairs.
recommendations.why: I fetched and parsed all of these. It solves four problems in one move: grammar count goes from ~20/level to 77/89/130/149/150 (N5..N1); furigana becomes correct ruby segmentation instead of a guessed kana alignment; vocab gets a frequency rank for ordering; and sentence-to-words makes offline i+1 selection a trivial set operation. OpenJLPT N5 has 163/662 entries with an EMPTY `reading` field, which silently breaks furigana, audio lookup, and reading-quiz cards.

recommendations.title: The daily loop: one 'Today' screen that runs Review → Learn → Apply → Mine, in that fixed order
recommendations.decision: Root screen is not a level picker, it is TODAY. It shows: (1) Reviews due [N] — always runs first, no new material is reachable until due=0 or the user explicitly skips; (2) Learn 10 new — hard cap, adaptively reduced (see the cap formula in code_or_data) when review backlog is high; (3) 1 grammar point + 5 cloze reps; (4) Apply: one 60-180s story or video clip built from words you already know + today's new ones; (5) Mine: the Apply step surfaces 1-3 tappable unknown words, one tap adds them to tomorrow's new queue. Target 15-20 min. Level pickers (N5..N1) live one level down as a Browse/Study-by-level surface.
recommendations.why: This is the intersection of every app that retains users. WaniKani forces reviews before lessons and level-ups are gated on Guru'ing 90% of the level's kanji. jpdb pulls new cards only in deck order and won't show deck 2 until deck 1 is exhausted. Satori Reader and LingQ put the mining step inside the reading step rather than in a separate 'add word' screen. Duolingo's own retention team found that separating the daily goal from the streak produced +3.3% D14 retention — i.e. the daily *unit of work* has to be a concrete finishable thing, which 'reviews to zero' is and 'study some' isn't.

recommendations.title: One word is several cards, not one — and cards must be dependency-gated
recommendations.decision: Generate 4 card types per vocab item: RECOGNITION (JA→EN, tap-to-reveal + 4-button self-grade), READING (kanji form → type/choose the kana), LISTENING (audio only → EN), PRODUCTION (EN + context sentence with a blank → assemble the JA from kana tiles). Enable recognition+listening from day one, unlock reading once the word's kanji are individually known, unlock production only at FSRS stability > ~21 days. Gate: a vocab card containing kanji K is LOCKED until K's own card has reached the 'known' threshold; a kanji card is locked until its radicals are known. Ship a `locked` card state exactly like jpdb's.
recommendations.why: jpdb explicitly enumerates Locked as a card state and decomposes vocabulary into kanji and components to teach 'bottom-up'. WaniKani requires both a meaning AND a reading answer per kanji and won't unlock kanji until the radicals are Guru. A single JA→EN card produces learners who 'know' 食べる but cannot read 食事 — this is the #1 complaint about homemade decks. Production-last matches the recognition-before-recall ordering that makes early progress feel fast.

recommendations.title: Use FSRS via ts-fsrs, with 4 grade buttons, not a homemade Leitner/SM-2
recommendations.decision: Import ts-fsrs 5.4.2 as an ES module from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ts-fsrs@latest/+esm (vendor the 23KB file into the repo so the app stays offline). Config: request_retention 0.90, enable_fuzz true, enable_short_term true, learning_steps ['1m','10m'], relearning_steps ['10m'], maximum_interval 365. Expose 4 buttons: Again / Hard / Good / Easy. Add a WaniKani-style human-readable stage label on top of FSRS stability so the user sees progress: Apprentice (S<1d) / Guru (1-14d) / Master (14-60d) / Enlightened (60-180d) / Burned (>180d), and surface a Burned counter.
recommendations.why: I verified ts-fsrs@5.4.2 serves as a 23,013-byte ESM bundle from jsDelivr (HTTP 200). FSRS models difficulty/stability/retrievability and handles lapses and irregular reviews far better than SM-2 — which matters enormously for a phone app that gets used erratically. The stage names are pure UI sugar but they are why WaniKani feels like progress and raw Anki does not: 'Burned' is a completion ceremony that an interval number in days can never be.

recommendations.title: Bake YouTube transcripts AND their tokenization at build time; never tokenize on the phone
recommendations.decision: Build step (Node): fetch the caption track via the ANDROID innertube player recipe from the shared context, prefer a manual (no `kind:'asr'`) ja track, then run kuromoji over each cue in Node and emit token arrays with dictionary-form lemmas. Ship per-video JSON: {videoId,title,level,cues:[{t,d,ja,en,tokens:[{s,surface,base,reading,pos,wordId|null}]}]}. At runtime the player just renders tokens as tappable spans — zero tokenizer on device. Tag each token with a wordId into the app's vocab DB so a tap opens the same word sheet used everywhere else, with a Save button.
recommendations.why: I measured kuromoji's dictionary: the dist JS is 308KB but the /dict directory is ~19MB of .gz files (base.dat.gz alone is 3.96MB). Shipping that to a phone is indefensible when the transcripts are already static and known at build time. Language Reactor and Migaku get their whole value from exactly this interaction — click a word in a subtitle, get a popup with the definition, save it with its context sentence — and Migaku's one-click save captures sentence + audio + translation together, which is the thing that makes mined words stick.

recommendations.title: Compute i+1 sentences offline and make them the backbone of Learn and Story
recommendations.decision: At build time, for every sentence S in data/corpus/sentences.json, look up its word IDs in data/cross-refs/sentence-to-words.json. For each vocab word W, precompute a shortlist of sentences where W appears and all other words fall below a low frequency rank / are in N5-N4 — i.e. candidate i+1 sentences ordered by 'how few other hard words'. Store 2-3 per word. At runtime, pick the candidate where the count of words the user hasn't unlocked is exactly 1 (that being W); fall back to the lowest-unknown-count candidate. Use the same index to assemble the per-level Short Story: greedily pick sentences that introduce at most one new word each.
recommendations.why: This is jpdb's headline feature — it tracks what you know so it can show only sentences where you know every word except the lookup word — and it is normally impossible without a server. The sentence-to-words mapping (verified: {"tatoeba-100041":["1206540","1332020","1517230"]}) makes it a static precomputation. It also turns the user's 'short story text' request from hand-written filler into automatically generated, always-level-appropriate content. Research consensus is 95-98% known-token coverage for unassisted comprehension; i+1 is the operational version of that.

recommendations.title: Audio-first vocab: bake JapanesePod101 mp3s where they exist, fall back to on-device speechSynthesis
recommendations.decision: Build step: for each vocab item request https://assets.languagepod101.com/dictionary/japanese/audiomp3.php?kanji=<word>&kana=<reading>; treat a response of EXACTLY 52,288 bytes as 'no audio' and discard it. Files are ~3-7KB each. Bake the hits into /audio/<hash>.mp3. At runtime: if a baked file exists play it; otherwise call speechSynthesis with a ja-JP voice (utterance.lang='ja-JP', pick a voice whose lang startsWith 'ja'). In every card, play audio BEFORE revealing the English.
recommendations.why: I verified this endpoint live: 食べる returned 2,760 bytes audio/mpeg, 水 returned 2,400 bytes, and a nonsense word returned exactly 52,288 bytes (the silent placeholder). Critically it sends NO Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, so the browser cannot fetch it at runtime — it must be baked. Coverage is only ~16/40 on an N5 sample (kana-only words like あさって, おいしい, いす are simply absent), hence the TTS fallback. Core 2k/6k, Renshuu (15,000+ native recordings) and Satori (tap any sentence for native voice actors) all treat audio as primary, not decoration.

recommendations.title: Grammar must be a typed/assembled cloze drill with SRS, not a reference list
recommendations.decision: Each grammar point gets: a short meaning line, formation, 2-3 example sentences with audio, formation_notes as 'watch out' bullets, and `related[]` as tap-through links (all present in the curated dataset). Its review card is a cloze: show the example sentence with the pattern blanked out plus the English, and have the user assemble the answer from kana/particle tiles (mobile-friendly substitute for typing). Add Bunpro-style 'ghost' handling: a point failed 3+ times gets a marker and a shortened, separate relearn schedule. Nest grammar SRS into the same Today queue as vocab.
recommendations.why: Bunpro's entire value proposition is that cloze deletion beats recognition for long-term retention, and its ghost mechanic exists because grammar failures cluster on a handful of points. Multiple-choice grammar creates false confidence — the learner recognizes the right answer without being able to produce it. Tile assembly preserves the production requirement while dodging the Japanese-IME-on-mobile problem, which is the single worst UX trap in this app category.

recommendations.title: Per-level home screen: ranked tile list (the user's four, plus seven more)
recommendations.decision: Order tiles exactly: 1) Study this level (feeds Today), 2) Words, 3) Kanji (radicals→kanji→vocab chain, with KanjiVG stroke-order animation), 4) Grammar, 5) Flashcards / My saved words, 6) Read (short stories, i+1 generated), 7) Watch (video + dual subs), 8) Listen (audio-only drill: hear word → pick meaning), 9) Conjugation drill (from data/grammar/conjugations.json), 10) Mock test (timed section practice), 11) Level progress (% of vocab/kanji/grammar at Guru+, 'exam readiness' meter). Show a per-tile progress ring so the level screen doubles as a dashboard. For N5 only, prepend a 0) Kana tile.
recommendations.why: Ranked by leverage. Kanji sits above grammar because JLPT reading is kanji-gated and because every other item in the app depends on kanji knowledge for its unlock state — Kanshudo maps its usefulness levels directly onto JLPT for exactly this reason. Listening is #8 only because it's cheap to build once audio is baked, but it's the skill self-study learners are weakest at. Conjugation drill earns its slot at N5/N4 specifically: te-form and the ます/plain split are where beginners stall, and they're drillable in a way vocab isn't. Mock test is last but non-negotiable if the user's frame is 'N5..N1'.

recommendations.title: Onboarding: 3-day timeboxed hiragana, katakana in parallel, romaji deleted on day 4
recommendations.decision: Day 0 (first 10 minutes, no account, no settings): 10 hiragana via mnemonic cards, then 3 real words built from them, then one readable sentence. End the first session with a visible win. Days 1-3: finish hiragana (46 base + dakuten + yōon) with recognition SRS. Day 4: katakana starts IN PARALLEL with the first N5 vocab — do not gate vocab behind katakana. Romaji is visible for days 0-3 only and is then permanently removed with an explicit 'romaji off' moment. Furigana defaults to ON and becomes adaptive (Satori-style: hide furigana per-kanji once that kanji is known), with a manual override of kanji / furigana / kana-only.
recommendations.why: Tofugu's path budgets hiragana at 1 day-1 week and katakana at 2 days-2 weeks with katakana explicitly overlapping early kanji study — katakana is slower to stick and gating on it stalls beginners for a fortnight. The user said 'fast', so the design constraint is that day 1 must produce a readable sentence. Adaptive furigana is Satori Reader's 'according to your knowledge' setting and is the single feature that lets the same text serve an N5 and an N3 learner.

recommendations.title: Basic→professional arc: five stages with a parallel Business track that forks at N3
recommendations.decision: A: kana + N5 (684 vocab / 79 kanji / 77 grammar) + survival phrases. B: N4 (640/166/89), master です・ます vs plain, 自己紹介. C: N3 (1730/367/130) — the bridge; FORK the Business track here with 丁寧語 discipline, 電話応対, and the three-way 尊敬語/謙譲語/丁寧語 model. D: N2 (1812/367/149) = the actual hiring bar; Business track goes full: email template assembly, 報連相, 会議, 名刺交換, 社内 vs 社外 register, and keigo for the three face-sensitive acts (依頼/謝罪/断り). E: N1 (3427/1232/150) + BJT prep + an industry vocab pack (IT / finance / manufacturing / medical). Business vocabulary domain order: self-intro & company hierarchy (部長/課長/係長) → time & scheduling → email formulae → phone → 報連相 / status reporting → requests, apologies, refusals → numbers, negotiation, contracts → industry domain.
recommendations.why: Business Japanese programs universally set entry at JLPT N2 / BJT J2 and describe 'business level' as keigo + email + meetings + business materials; BJT itself tests situational judgment ('what do you say here'), not grammar knowledge, and a ~30-hour prep course moves scores 60-80 points. Forking at N3 rather than N2 is my opinionated deviation: keigo takes far longer than its grammar complexity suggests because it's a register habit, and starting exposure at N3 while formal study waits for N2 costs nothing.

recommendations.title: Build keigo as a transformation drill and business email as template assembly — never as flashcard decks
recommendations.decision: Keigo module: a conjugation-style drill with four columns — plain / 丁寧 / 尊敬 / 謙譲 — prompting e.g. 言う → 言います / おっしゃる / 申す・申し上げる. Same tile-assembly UI as grammar cloze. Cover the ~20 irregular pairs first (言う, 見る, 行く, 来る, いる, する, 食べる, 知る, もらう, あげる, ある...), then the productive ご/お〜になる and お〜する patterns. Email module: a slot-filling builder — 宛名 / 挨拶 (お世話になっております) / 名乗り / 用件 / 依頼 or 報告 / 結び (何卒よろしくお願いいたします) / 署名 — where the user picks a register and a situation and assembles the mail from phrase blocks, then compares to a model.
recommendations.why: This is the one place where every generic app fails and where a purpose-built tool wins. Keigo failure isn't 'I don't know おっしゃる', it's 'I can't convert under time pressure' — which is a drill, not a recall problem. Business email is formulaic to the point of being a grammar of its own; Japanese professionals assemble mails from fixed blocks, so teaching the blocks and the slots is teaching the real skill. Coto's and KAI's business courses are structured exactly this way (keigo drills + weekly email writing + timed reading/listening sets).

recommendations.title: Gamification: streak + freezes + review-to-zero + level ceremony. Skip leagues, hearts, XP, shops.
recommendations.decision: Build: (a) a daily streak with 2-3 earnable streak freezes, auto-spent; (b) a daily goal (e.g. 'finish reviews + 10 new') tracked and displayed SEPARATELY from the streak; (c) the due counter driven to zero as the primary session goal, shown everywhere; (d) a GitHub-style review heatmap; (e) a Burned/Mastered counter that only goes up; (f) a full-screen level-up ceremony when a level's kanji hit 90% Guru+; (g) navigator.setAppBadge(dueCount) so the home-screen icon carries the due count. Do NOT build leaderboards, leagues, hearts/lives, XP inflation, or gem shops.
recommendations.why: Duolingo's retention team calls the streak 'the single most effective retention lever', measured +3.3% D14 retention and +10.5% streak-holders from raising the freeze cap from 1 to 2-3, and got the same +3.3% from splitting the daily goal from the streak. Everything I dropped is either social (impossible with no server), punitive (hearts exist to sell refills), or noise. The badge API is the key substitute for push: it needs no server, works on an installed PWA on Android and iOS 16.4+, and reproduces the one notification that actually matters — 'you have 23 reviews'.

recommendations.title: Adaptive new-card cap, leech handling, and a hard 'never let the backlog spiral' rule
recommendations.decision: newToday = clamp(0, 10, 10 - floor(dueCount / 25)) — so at 250 due, new cards stop entirely. Show the user why ('Catch up on reviews to unlock new words'). Any card failed 5+ times becomes a LEECH: pull it out of the main queue, re-teach it with a fresh mnemonic and a different example sentence, and offer a Suspend button. Add a 'Never forget' / retire state (jpdb has this) so the deck doesn't grow forever. Add a vacation/pause mode that freezes scheduling instead of building debt.
recommendations.why: The #1 reason self-study SRS users quit is the 400-reviews-due death spiral after one missed week. WaniKani's fixed lesson batch (default 5, range 3-10) and jpdb's deck-order gating are both throttles in disguise. Leeches are ~10% of cards but consume a disproportionate share of review time; Bunpro's ghost mechanic and Anki's leech tagging both exist to quarantine them. Without these, the app is great for three weeks and abandoned in month two.

recommendations.title: Word detail sheet: one component, one field order, reachable from everywhere
recommendations.decision: Field order top to bottom: [big word in kanji with ruby furigana] · [pitch-accent-marked reading] · [play audio button] · [1-3 English meanings, numbered] · [part of speech + JLPT level chip + frequency rank chip] · [Save / Learning / Known state toggle] · [kanji breakdown — each kanji tappable, with its radicals] · [2 example sentences with per-sentence English + audio + tappable words] · [conjugation table if verb/adj] · [related words sharing a kanji]. Open it as a bottom sheet (thumb-reachable), never a full page navigation, so tapping a word inside a subtitle or story never loses the reading position.
recommendations.why: Every app converges on roughly this order and the bottom sheet is the load-bearing UX decision: Language Reactor, Migaku, Todai and Satori all use a non-navigating popup precisely because navigating away from the video/text kills the reading flow. Migaku's inclusion of pitch accent is worth copying — Kanjium data is available and it's the field learners regret skipping. The frequency chip is Kanshudo's 'usefulness' idea and answers the user's implicit question 'is this worth learning?'

recommendations.title: Ship an export/import backup button on day one
recommendations.decision: A Settings > Backup screen with 'Download my data' (a single .json of saved words, all FSRS card states, streak, settings) and 'Restore from file'. Auto-prompt a backup every 30 days. Store study state in IndexedDB, not localStorage.
recommendations.why: This is the highest-regret item in the whole build. iOS Safari's storage eviction can clear site data after ~7 days without interaction, and while installed Home Screen web apps are treated more favourably, the behaviour has changed repeatedly across iOS versions and is not something to bet a year of the user's saved vocabulary on. localStorage also has a ~5MB ceiling and is synchronous, which will jank the review UI. The user explicitly asked to save words 'for later' — losing that list once ends the app's life.

recommendations.title: Treat the video module as online-only and verify every video at build time
recommendations.decision: Mark the Watch tile with an offline indicator and degrade it gracefully when navigator.onLine is false (the baked transcript still works as a readable, tappable dual-language transcript with no video). In the build pipeline, run every candidate videoId through https://www.youtube.com/oembed?url=...&format=json and drop any that 404; re-run this check on every build. Prefer manual caption tracks and label auto-generated ones ('auto-captions — may contain errors'). Render your own subtitle overlay from the baked cues and hide YouTube's native captions via the IFrame API (cc_load_policy=0), because you need big, dual-language, per-word-tappable text that YouTube's renderer cannot give you.
recommendations.why: The rest of the app is genuinely offline; the YouTube iframe is not, and pretending otherwise produces a broken screen on the subway. oEmbed is the cheap liveness check. Auto-generated Japanese ASR has no word boundaries and frequently mis-segments, which poisons the tap-a-word feature — so preferring manual tracks isn't a nicety, it's what makes the headline interaction trustworthy. Building your own overlay is also the only way to satisfy the user's 'big subtitles, both languages, pause anytime, tap any word'.

recommendations.title: Mobile UX: bottom nav, thumb-zone controls, one-hand review, 44px+ targets
recommendations.decision: Bottom tab bar: Today / Levels / Saved / Stats. Review screen: card content in the upper two-thirds, grade buttons pinned to the bottom third within thumb reach, swipe-right = Good, swipe-left = Again, tap card = reveal. Japanese text at 28-40px minimum (furigana at ~50% of base). Respect env(safe-area-inset-bottom). Full-screen, portrait-locked video page with the subtitle block BELOW the video (not overlaid) so it can be large and tappable, and a fat pause bar. Haptic feedback on grade via navigator.vibrate where available.
recommendations.why: The user's first sentence was 'I will be using on my phone'. Review sessions are 100-300 taps long, so a mis-sized tap target is a per-session tax. Putting subtitles below the video rather than over it is the specific deviation from desktop tools like Language Reactor that phone form factor forces — overlaid dual-language subtitles at readable size would cover the video entirely.

recommendations.title: Attribution page (license compliance, not optional)
recommendations.decision: A Settings > Credits screen listing: JMdict/JMnedict (EDRDG, CC-BY-SA 4.0), KANJIDIC2 (EDRDG), KanjiVG (CC-BY-SA 3.0), Tatoeba (CC-BY 2.0 FR), Kanjium pitch accent, JmdictFurigana, Jonathan Waller's JLPT lists (CC-BY 4.0, tanos.co.uk), jkindrix/japanese-language-data (CC-BY-SA 4.0), OpenJLPT (CC-BY-SA 4.0). State that derived data is redistributed under CC-BY-SA 4.0.
recommendations.why: CC-BY-SA 4.0 is share-alike with an attribution requirement; the aggregate dataset's own README is explicit that derivatives must carry the same license. It's a 20-minute screen that makes the app legitimately shareable.

verified_facts.claim: jkindrix/japanese-language-data hosts a unified CC-BY-SA 4.0 Japanese dataset with grammar, furigana, pitch accent, frequency, radicals, stroke order, JLPT classifications and sentence cross-references — all raw-fetchable
verified_facts.evidence: GitHub contents API listing of data/: core, corpus, cross-refs, enrichment, grammar, optional. Verified files include data/enrichment/furigana.json (7,084,733 B), pitch-accent.json (17,768,044 B), frequency-corpus.json (1,612,072 B), jlpt-classifications.json (2,459,279 B), stroke-order-index.json (1,236,536 B), data/corpus/sentences.json (9,885,004 B), data/cross-refs/sentence-to-words.json (755,095 B), data/grammar/conjugations.json (4,677,057 B), data/core/radicals.json (1,795,816 B). README confirms CC-BY-SA 4.0 end-to-end and sources: JMdict, KANJIDIC2, KanjiVG, Tatoeba, Kanjium, Waller.

verified_facts.claim: That repo's curated grammar set has 595 points across N5-N1, roughly 5x OpenJLPT's, with rich fields
verified_facts.evidence: Parsed grammar-curated/n{5,4,3,2,1}.json: N5=77, N4=89, N3=130, N2=149, N1=150, total 595. Sample entry keys: id, pattern, level, meaning_en, meaning_detailed, formation, formation_notes[], formality, related[], examples[{japanese,english,source}], review_status, sources[]. Caveat: every entry is review_status:'draft' and the README states it is not native-speaker reviewed.

verified_facts.claim: Waller-derived JLPT classifications give 11,099 leveled items with per-kind counts
verified_facts.evidence: Parsed data/enrichment/jlpt-classifications.json. vocab N5=684 N4=640 N3=1730 N2=1812 N1=3427; kanji N5=79 N4=166 N3=367 N2=367 N1=1232; grammar N5=77 N4=89 N3=130 N2=149 N1=150. metadata.source = 'Jonathan Waller JLPT Resources, via stephenmk/yomitan-jlpt-vocab and davidluzgouveia/kanji-data', license CC-BY 4.0 / CC-BY-SA 4.0.

verified_facts.claim: Offline i+1 sentence selection is computable: the dataset ships a sentence→word-ID mapping alongside the sentence corpus
verified_facts.evidence: data/cross-refs/sentence-to-words.json shape: {metadata, mapping:{"tatoeba-100041":["1206540","1332020","1517230"], ...}}. data/corpus/sentences.json shape: {metadata, sentences:[{id:'tatoeba-4711', japanese, english, curated, license_flag:'CC-BY-2.0-FR', has_audio}]}. Word IDs are JMdict seq numbers, which also appear as jmdict_seq in jlpt-classifications.json — so the join is direct.

verified_facts.claim: furigana.json gives pre-segmented ruby, removing the need to align kanji to kana yourself
verified_facts.evidence: {metadata, entries:[28920]}; sample entry {"text":"ＣＤプレーヤー","reading":"シーディープレーヤー","segments":[{"ruby":"Ｃ","rt":"シー"},{"ruby":"Ｄ","rt":"ディー"},{"ruby":"プレーヤー"}]} — segments with no rt are plain text, segments with rt become <ruby>.

verified_facts.claim: ts-fsrs is usable in a no-build static app straight from jsDelivr as an ES module
verified_facts.evidence: GET https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ts-fsrs@latest/+esm → HTTP 200, 23,013 bytes. Body header: 'Bundled by jsDelivr ... Original file: /npm/ts-fsrs@5.4.2/dist/index.mjs'. npm registry confirms latest = 5.4.2.

verified_facts.claim: JapanesePod101 word audio is fetchable at build time, has a detectable 'missing' sentinel, but is CORS-blocked and only ~40% covers N5
verified_facts.evidence: 食べる → HTTP 200, 2,760 B, audio/mpeg. 水 → 200, 2,400 B. Nonsense word ほげほげほげ → 200, exactly 52,288 B (the silent placeholder). function pickSentence(wordId, known /* Set of wordIds */) {

  for (const sid of c) {
    const unknown = S2W[sid].filter(w => w !== wordId && !known.has(w));

risks: OpenJLPT N5 has 163 of 662 entries with an EMPTY `reading` field, and some `word` values contain a slash ("いい/よい"). Naive code will render broken furigana, build malformed audio URLs, and generate unanswerable reading cards. Either switch to the Waller-derived jlpt-classifications.json (which has a reading on every row) or explicitly handle reading==='' by falling back to the word itself and splitting on '/'.

The JapanesePod101 audio endpoint sends NO Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. Any runtime fetch() or <audio src> cross-origin read will fail in the browser. It MUST be baked at build time. It also silently returns a 52,288-byte placeholder for missing words instead of a 404 — checking response.ok will happily cache thousands of identical silent clips.

Coverage of that audio is only ~40% on an N5 sample and it is systematically missing the kana-only everyday words (あさって, おいしい, いす, あなた). If you ship audio-first cards without the speechSynthesis fallback, the most common beginner words will be the silent ones — the exact opposite of what you want.

Do not ship kuromoji to the phone. The dictionary is ~19 MB gzipped (base.dat.gz alone is 3.96 MB) on top of a 308 KB tokenizer. Tokenize subtitles and story text in Node at build time and ship token arrays. If someone later wants runtime tokenization for pasted text, that is a separate, opt-in download — not the default.

iOS Safari storage eviction is the single biggest data-loss risk. Site data can be cleared after ~7 days of non-use, and the exemptions for installed Home Screen web apps have shifted across iOS releases. Use IndexedDB (not localStorage, which is synchronous and ~5 MB), and ship export/import backup from v1. The user explicitly asked to save words for later — losing that list once kills the app.

The YouTube iframe makes the Watch module online-only, which breaks the offline-first promise unless you handle it. Detect navigator.onLine and degrade to a tappable transcript view. Also note that an installed PWA on iOS gets no background sync and no scheduled local notifications without a push server — navigator.setAppBadge is the only no-server reminder mechanism, and you should verify it on the actual device rather than trusting the support matrix.

Auto-generated (kind:'asr') Japanese caption tracks have no word boundaries and mis-segment frequently, and &tlang=en English is machine translation. If you tokenize an ASR track you will attach confident-looking definitions to wrong word boundaries — the worst possible failure for the headline tap-a-word feature. Prefer manual tracks, and label ASR/machine content in the UI.

Curated videos rot. Videos get deleted, made private, or region-locked, and a dead iframe is a dead screen. Run the oembed check on every build and keep at least 3 videos per level so one death is not fatal.

The 595 curated grammar points are all marked review_status:'draft' and the upstream README states plainly that they have not been reviewed by native-speaker linguists. They are far better than nothing and better than OpenJLPT's ~20/level, but do not present them as authoritative; spot-check N5/N4 against JLPT Sensei or Bunpro's public point lists before shipping.
CC-BY-SA 4.0 is share-alike with an attribution requirement, and the Tatoeba sentences carry CC-BY-2.0-FR separately. A Credits screen is a licence obligation, not a nicety.

Review-debt spiral is the predictable month-two failure. Without the adaptive new-card cap, leech quarantine, a never-forget/retire state, and a pause mode, the app will feel excellent for three weeks and then present 400 due cards and get deleted.

Do not implement grammar or vocab answers as multiple choice. It is the easy mobile input and it produces measurable false confidence — learners pass the card and cannot produce the word. Use tap-to-reveal self-grading for meaning and tile assembly for production.

Do not let romaji become a permanent display mode or an accessibility setting. Once it exists as a toggle, beginners never turn it off and kana reading never becomes automatic. Make removing it a dated, one-way, celebrated event on day 4.

Resist shipping all 8,000+ words as one JSON. Chunk content per level and lazy-load through the Cache API, or first paint on a mid-range Android phone will take seconds and the install will be enormous. Budget: initial install under ~5 MB, total after all levels cached under ~50 MB.
